title: The familiar display name — question explanation
learningObjective: Check the actual sender address and domain rather than relying on display name
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: An email displays the name “Campus IT Helpdesk,” but the full sender address ends in an unrelated public email domain. It asks you to confirm your password.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Check the actual sender address and domain rather than relying on display name
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option A: The full sender address and domain, checked against a known official contact. Inspect the full address and verify the domain using an independently known directory or channel.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option B: Display names are easy to choose or imitate and do not authenticate the sender. Option C: Timing is weak evidence; malicious messages can be sent at any time. Option D: Logos can be copied and are not proof of message origin.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Expand sender details, inspect the full address and domain, and contact IT through the published helpdesk channel if a credential request is unexpected. A familiar name or logo is not identity proof; inspect and independently verify the actual address.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.

narration: Scenario: An email displays the name “Campus IT Helpdesk,” but the full sender address ends in an unrelated public email domain. It asks you to confirm your password. Inspect the full address and verify the domain using an independently known directory or channel. Option C is unsafe because Timing is weak evidence; malicious messages can be sent at any time. Option D is unsafe because Logos can be copied and are not proof of message origin. In practice: Expand sender details, inspect the full address and domain, and contact IT through the published helpdesk channel if a credential request is unexpected. Key takeaway: A familiar name or logo is not identity proof; inspect and independently verify the actual address.
